newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom urges "round table" on cable TV.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom urges "round table" on cable TV.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG , the German phone giant, said on Thursday it had invited representatives of media, government and other telecommunications companies to round table talks on the future of cable television.

The invitation follows months of frustrating negotiations with broadcasters and regulators over Telekom's efforts to revamp billing structures to account for digital television and the failure so far to agree a standard for digital TV decoders.
Telekom would not give any details about specific issues to be talked about during the discussions, which it said could begin in mid-May.
"I am certain that we can develope a model that would be a compromise for all parties when seen from each one's particular perspective," said Telekom chairman Ron Sommer in a statement.
"But when viewed from a broader economic perspective it would be seen as an exceptional solution."

Telekom said that if "all parties worked constructively" on the proposals, new models for cable television in the age of digital transmission technology could be presented at this summer's International Broadcasting Exhibition in Berlin.
Deutsche Telekom is the only company in Germany that owns and operates a national cable television backbone network, which connects some 17 million homes.
Because there is competition at the local network level, Telekom has just under six million subcribers under direct contract.

The rest are controlled by various regional and local cable TV operators, such as O.Tel.O, the telecoms venture of utilities RWE AG and Veba AG, which has around two million cable TV subscribers and is the number two after Telekom.
In the past, media regulators have determined what would be shown on cable television and Telekom and the other operators have had little influence in the choice of programming.
But now Telekom wants to change the model.

Instead of receiving fees from broadcasters it carries, Telekom wants to adopt the model practised in the United States and Britain, where the operator buys programming but then takes a share of the lucrative advertising and subscription revenues.
Under the new system Telekom envisions, it would package the programming and sell it in various billing plans, but would have direct responsibility for subsrcriber management itself.

Commercial pay TV broadcasters, such as Premiere with 1.4 million subscribers, shudder at the thought of having to share subscription revenues with Telekom and at the idea giving up control of their customers.

Media regulators have encouraged the new model because it would allow Telekom to better refinance investment in the cable network. With its modernisation programme, Telekom now has 150 digital channels and around 30 analogue channels.

But media regulators also want to be able to determine that there are a certain number of so-called "must carry" stations, largely public broadcasters, that cable operators would be required to carry in their networks.
